summary:
ABANDONED BUT NOT FORGOTTEN is an interactive educational website and digital comic-book series that explores the stories of spacecraft, landers, rovers and scientific instruments left behind during humanity’s exploration of space.

Designed to make space science engaging and accessible, particularly for students aged 10–16, the project takes visitors on a journey across the Moon, Mars and Deep Space. It highlights missions such as Apollo, Surveyor, Sojourner, Viking, InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker and Kepler, explaining their discoveries, achievements and lasting contributions to science.

The project combines a website built using HTML, CSS and JavaScript with illustrated digital comic books inspired by the vintage comic-book style of the 1960s and 1970s. NASA mission archives, scientific resources and imagery help support the factual content, while storytelling and visual design bring these historic missions to life.

The central idea is to show that even when a mission ends, its discoveries and contributions continue to shape our understanding of the universe. By turning forgotten space explorers into the heroes of their own stories, the project aims to inspire curiosity, encourage interest in STEM and remind audiences that every space mission leaves behind a meaningful legacy.
details:
ABANDONED BUT NOT FORGOTTEN

ABANDONED BUT NOT FORGOTTEN is an interactive, web-based educational project that explores the stories of spacecraft, rovers, landers and scientific instruments left behind across the Moon, Mars and Deep Space after their missions.

The project aims to introduce school-age students, particularly those aged 10–16, and general space enthusiasts to the history and scientific achievements of these robotic explorers.

The website organises the experience into three main areas: Moon, Mars and Deep Space. Visitors can navigate through different missions and explore their histories through digital comic books, illustrations and educational content.

Our Moon section highlights missions such as Apollo and Surveyor, along with the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP). The Mars section explores missions such as NASA's InSight lander and the scientific instruments that studied the Martian interior. The Deep Space section features Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker and Kepler, showcasing their contributions to planetary science, asteroid exploration and the discovery of exoplanets.

The project combines a website with downloadable digital comic books to make complex scientific information more accessible and engaging. Rather than presenting mission histories as technical lists, we use a vintage 1960s–1970s comic-book-inspired storytelling approach to make each mission feel like an exploration adventure.

The main benefit of the project is that it connects scientific discoveries with the stories of the machines that made them possible. It encourages curiosity, improves awareness of space exploration history and demonstrates that even when a mission ends, its scientific legacy continues.

Our intended impact is to inspire the next generation to appreciate space science, understand the engineering behind robotic exploration and become interested in future scientific discoveries.

Technologies and tools used:

  • HTML for the website structure.
  • CSS for styling, layouts and visual design.
  • JavaScript for navigation and interactive functionality.
  • NASA APIs and publicly available NASA mission resources for research and imagery.
  • PDF format for the digital comic books.
  • GitHub for source-code management.
  • Vercel for website deployment.
  • AI-assisted tools for brainstorming, coding assistance, debugging and selected visual-design tasks.

The creative aspect of our project lies in presenting abandoned space hardware as more than forgotten machinery. Each spacecraft has a history, a purpose and a scientific legacy. By combining accurate mission information with comic-book-inspired storytelling, we aim to give these silent explorers a lasting voice.

During development, we considered the target age group, accessibility through a web browser, clarity of scientific explanations, historical accuracy, visual engagement and the importance of distinguishing completed missions from spacecraft that remain in orbit or continue travelling through space.
